background.definition: Poliomyelitis can be a crippling paralytic disease caused by the polioviruses. Polio infection is acquired by fecal-oral transmission or from live virus vaccinations. Post-polio syndrome is characterized by new neurologic symptoms that appear several years after an initial paralytic polio infection.

list.listitem: The polio virus is spread in two ways: wild-type transmission and circulating vaccine-derived polio. The latter is rare and happens when vaccine prevalence is low and the live vaccine virus reverts to neurovirulence.

In 2020, there were 140 cases of wild-type polio reported from the remaining two endemic countries, Afghanistan and Pakistan. In August 2020, the Africa region was declared free of wild-type polio transmission. Since 2017, the number of circulating vaccine-derived polio has increased. In 2020, the number of countries reporting this type of outbreak grew to 32.
Polio infection was eradicated in the Americas in 1991.
About 1/3 of patients with paralytic polio infection will develop post-polio syndrome within 30 to 40 years.
Poliovirus is a member of the enterovirus subgroup, family Picornaviridae.
Picornaviruses are small viruses with an RNA genome.
There are 3 poliovirus serotypes (P1, P2, and P3).
Polio is quickly inactivated by heat, formaldehyde, chlorine, and ultraviolet light.
In addition to natural infection, in rare cases the live oral polio vaccination can also cause paralytic polio.

Oral poliovirus vaccine causes virus to be excreted in the stool of the vaccinated person for up to 6 weeks. Persons coming in contact with fecal material of a vaccinated person may be exposed and infected with vaccine virus.

Clinical manifestations of poliovirus infection range from asymptomatic to flu-like symptoms to flaccid paralysis of a single limb or quadriplegia, respiratory failure, and death. Most of those infected will be completely asymptomatic, the rest will develop flu-like illness and only 1% will develop neurologic complications from an acute infection.
It is transmitted fecal-orally and once it enters the mouth, it multiplies in the pharynx and gastrointestinal tract.
It is highly contagious, and is most contagious in the 10 days before and after start of symptoms. Infected persons can be shed the virus for weeks in their feces.
The virus invades local lymphoid tissue, enters the blood, and may then infect the central nervous system.
Humans are the only reservoir of poliovirus.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Living with or caring for someone infected with the polio virus
Onset of polio under 12 months of age

list.listitem: All children should receive IPV at the ages of 2, 4, 6 to 18 months, and 4 to 6 years. In 2009, the CDC updated recommendations for routine polio vaccination emphasizing the importance of a booster dose at the age of at least 4 years, extending the minimum interval from dose 3 to dose 4 from 4 weeks to 6 months, and adding a precaution for the use of minimum intervals in the first 6 months of life. A

Adults who have received the childhood series should receive a single booster with IPV if they are traveling to polio-endemic areas or if they are going to be working with people or specimens potentially infected with polioviruses. C
Unvaccinated adults who are at increased risk should receive a primary vaccination series with IPV. C
Contraindications to the vaccine include allergy to streptomycin, neomycin, and polymyxin B (vaccine components) or severe allergic reaction to a previous dose of vaccine. C
A systematic review found no evidence of waning immunity from polio vaccines.

A randomized trial in Bangladesh compared strategies for catch-up immunization in infants 9 to 13 months of age. They concluded that immunization at an older age with 2 fractional doses of IPV was most immunogenic.
Collect at least two stool specimens and two throat swab specimens, each separated by 24 hours, from patients who are suspected to have polio. C

Suspect post-polio syndrome in patients with prior paralytic polio infection who had partial or complete recovery and after at least 15 years of functional stability develop new neuromuscular dysfunction. C

Refer patients with suspected post-polio syndrome for electromyography to establish the presence of lower motor neuron involvement, to identify the presence of other causes, and to assess the degree of neuron loss. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Pain or stiffness in the back, neck, arms, or legs; muscle spasms
Headache, fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, meningismus, muscle pain

list.listitem: According to the CDC web site, about 72% of people infected with polio will be asymptomatic, approximately 25% will develop a flu-like illness, and fewer than one percent will develop neurologic complications. These complications include menigitis and paralysis.
Progression to maximum paralysis is rapid (2-4 days) and is associated with fever and muscle pain.
Paralytic polio begins with fever then 5 to 7 days later people develop headache, neck and back stiffness, constipation, and increased sensitivity to touch.
When acute flaccid paralysis develops, it presents suddenly and is usually worse on one side of the body.
Paralytic polio is divided into three types: spinal, bulbar, and spinobulbar, depending on which body part is affected.

Spinal paralysis is typically asymmetric and more severe proximally. It may cause paralysis of the muscles that control breathing and those in the arms and legs. Deep tendon reflexes are absent or diminished.
Bulbar polio affects the brainstem and can compromise cranial nerves and affect swallowing and breathing. Spinobulbar polio is a combination of both bulbar and spinal paralytic polio.

Suspect post-polio syndrome in patients with prior paralytic polio infection wartial or fairly complete recovery who, after a period of at least 15 years of functional stability, develop gradual or abrupt onset of new neuromuscular dysfunction (weakness, atrophy, muscle pain, and muscle fatigue). The physical examination will often reveal diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes and normal sensation
To confirm the diagnosis of acute polio infection, the polio virus can be identified in throat secretions, stool, or cerebrospinal fluid. The greatest yield of virus is from stool.
The CDC recommends collecting at least two stool specimens and two throat swab specimens, each separated by 24 hours, from patients who are suspected to have polio.
A single stool specimen will identify about 81% of patients with acute polio infection. Adding a second stool specimen allows 96% of these patients to be identified.

Additionally, the CDC recommends acute and convalescent phase serum, collected 3 weeks later, for neutralizing antibodies. A 4-fold rise in antibody titer between appropriately timed acute-phase and convalescent-phase serum specimens is diagnostic for poliovirus infection.
In patients with post-polio syndrome, electromyography and histological tests of affected muscles reveal chronic and active denervation with reinnervation.
About 90% of patients with post-polio syndrome with objective muscle weakness have electromyographic evidence of denervation.

Suspect post-polio syndrome in patients with prior polio infection who had partial or complete recovery and after at least 15 years of functional stability develop gradual or abrupt onset of new neuromuscular dysfunction.
Clinical assessment of musculoskeletal strength, even when optimally standardized using a dynamometer, is quite variable.
Refer these patients for electromyography to establish the presence of lower motor neuron involvement, to identify the presence of other causes, and to assess the degree of neuron loss.
The treatment of acute polio infection is supportive: increasing comfort and preventing complications. C
There is no evidence of benefit for pyridostigmine, steroids, amantadine, and modafinil in patients with post-polio syndrome. B

A 2015 Cochrane review stated that definitive conclusions are not possible regarding the treatment of post-polio syndrome due to lack of good-quality data, but lamotrigine (for decreasing pan and fatigue), muscle strengthening exercises and static magnetic fields (both for improving muscle strength and pain) may be beneficial.
Biphasic-positive pressure and intermittent-positive pressure ventilation improve pulmonary function in patients with post-polio syndrome. B
Isokinetic and isometric exercise prevents further decline in muscle strength and can reduce muscle fatigue, weakness, and pain in patients with slight or moderate muscle weakness. B
Although a few trials have assessed pyridostigmine, steroids, and amantadine in patients with post-polio syndrome, none have found definitive benefit.
Modafinil was no better than placebo in treating the fatigue in patients with post-polio syndrome.
A single trial found that lamotrigine may improve pain and fatigue.

Compared with placebo, intravenous immunoglobulin modestly increases tests of muscle strength and vitality scores, but had no effect on sleep quality, overall symptoms and function, or pain. A Cochrane review found no overall evidence of benefit.
Respiratory aids, such as biphasic-positive pressure and intermittent-positive pressure ventilation, improve pulmonary function.
Isokinetic and isometric exercise prevents further decline in muscle strength and can reduce muscle fatigue, weakness, and pain in patients with slight or moderate muscle weakness.
Respiratory muscle training improves pulmonary function.
In a small RCT, there was no effect of coenzyme Q10 supplementation during resistance training on post-polio syndrome symptoms.
The treatment of acute polio infection is supportive: increasing comfort and preventing complications.
Supportive treatments include the following: antibiotics for secondary infections, analgesics for pain, portable ventilators to assist breathing, moderate exercise, and a nutritious diet.

In one case series, an aerobic exercise program in patients with post-polio syndrome resulted in improved fatigue and quality of life (home and hospital exercise groups) and increased functional capacity (hospital exercise group).
A single case of paralytic poliomyelitis demands immediate attention.
Collect preliminary vaccine history and contact information including exposure to oral polio.

Any case of suspected polio should be reported immediately. The CDC Emergency Operations Center can provide guidance. The number is 770.488.7100. The CDC also provides a suspected polio worksheet. The case should also be reported to the state health department.
Paralytic polio is fatal in 2% to 10% of cases.
After the acute episode, most patients recover at least some muscle function and recover within 6 months.
Post-polio syndrome affects about 1/3 of people who have recovered from polio. B

A systematic review of 19 studies found inconsistent results on functional outcomes of patients with post-polio syndrome. Nonetheless, it appears that the rate of decline in muscle strength is slow, and prognostic factors have not yet been identified. B

The development of vaccines against poliomyelitis has made it possible to control and contain the virus. The inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) was developed in the 1950s followed by the oral polio vaccine (OPV) in the 1960s. The IPV uses inactivated virus whereas the OPV relies on live attenuated virus. Compared to the IPV, the OPV induces a higher seroconversion rate, better intenstinal immunity and provides community protection through secondary shedding. For those reasons and the fact that it is cheaper and easier to deliver, it has been the preferred vaccination in endemic areas. In rare cases, however, the attenuated virus can revert to neurovirulence and cause vaccine-associated paralytic polio in vaccine recipients or their contacts.

In 1988, the Global Polio Eradication Initiative began to organize worldwide efforts to eradicate polio completely. Currently, most industrialized, polio-free countries use IPV-only immunization programs while developing countries at higher risk of polio outbreaks continue to use OPV. Challenges to eradication efforts include inability to deliver vaccines to young children, delayed response to outbreaks, and public distrust of immunization campaigns.
Recent polio research focuses on the development of more effective OPVs, approaches to outbreak containment, and optimal vaccination protocols in developing countries.
